definition: Automated essay scoring (AES) is the use of specialized computer programs to assign grades to essays written in an educational setting.
details: It is a form of educational assessment and an application of natural language processing. Its objective is to classify a large set of textual entities into a small number of discrete categories, corresponding to the possible grades, for example, the numbers 1 to 6. Therefore, it can be considered a problem of statistical classification. Several factors have contributed to a growing interest in AES. Among them are cost, accountability, standards, and technology. Rising education costs have led to pressure to hold the educational system accountable for results by imposing standards. The advance of information technology promises to measure educational achievement at reduced cost. The use of AES for high-stakes testing in education has generated significant backlash, with opponents pointing to research that computers cannot yet grade writing accurately and arguing that their use for such purposes promotes teaching writing in reductive ways (i.e. teaching to the test).

explainer.lead: Automated essay scoring uses computer programs to assign grades to student essays. It promises to assess writing at lower cost, but its use in high-stakes testing is controversial because of concerns about grading accuracy and narrower writing instruction.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a computer acting like a grader and putting each essay into one of a few score buckets, such as 1 through 6. This can help schools grade many essays, but people disagree about whether computers judge writing well enough for important tests.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer can frame AES as a natural language processing classification task within an educational assessment system, mapping each essay to one grade from a fixed set. High-stakes deployment requires caution because opponents cite inaccurate grading of writing and warn that AES can encourage teaching to the test.
tiers.paperLevel: AES maps a large set of essay texts X to a small discrete set of grades G, such as G = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, making it a statistical classification problem. Known concerns include whether computers can grade writing accurately and whether high-stakes use promotes reductive writing instruction.

explainer.example: For a test with six possible grades, an AES program reads each submitted essay and assigns it one grade from 1 to 6, sorting a large collection of essays into six score categories.

explainer.intuition: Instead of treating every essay as requiring a unique human-written evaluation, AES places it into one of a small number of grade categories. This turns large-scale essay grading into a classification task.
howItWorks: Collect a set of essays to be graded.
Give the essay texts to a specialized scoring program.
Treat the possible grades as discrete categories.
Classify each essay into one grade category.
explainer.whyItMatters: Interest in AES has grown alongside concerns about education costs, accountability, standards, and advances in information technology, with the promise of measuring achievement at reduced cost. Its high-stakes use matters just as much because of the backlash over accuracy and its possible effects on how writing is taught.
misconceptions: AES assigns grades; that does not establish that it accurately judges every aspect of writing.
Its use in high-stakes testing is contested, not universally accepted.
